title: The Sun of Righteousness and the Coming of Elijah
summary: The day is coming that will burn like a furnace, leaving the arrogant and evildoers like stubble with neither root nor branch. For those who fear God's name, the sun of righteousness will rise with healing in its wings, and they will leap like calves let out of the stall. The book closes by calling Israel to remember the law of Moses and promising that God will send Elijah the prophet before the great day of the LORD, to turn the hearts of fathers and children to one another.
story: In Hebrew Bibles these six verses are the end of chapter 3 (3:19-24), and they complete the argument that began at 3:13, where some said it was futile to serve God. Chapter 3 answered that the LORD would distinguish between the righteous and the wicked; chapter 4 shows what that distinction looks like on the day itself. Then the book, and the whole collection of the prophets, closes with two words: look back to Moses, and look forward to Elijah. For Christian readers these are the last words of the Old Testament before a long prophetic silence of about four hundred years. The next voice in the canon is Matthew's, and within three chapters a man dressed like Elijah is preaching repentance by the Jordan.
historical: The setting is the same Persian-period Judah of the mid-fifth century BC as the rest of the book, a community discouraged by delay and divided between cynics and the faithful. The hope of Elijah's return grew out of the way his earthly life ended: he did not die but was taken up to heaven in a whirlwind (2 Kings 2:11). Malachi's promise gave that hope a shape, and it shaped Jewish expectation for centuries. The book of Sirach, written in Hebrew in the early second century BC, praises Elijah as the one appointed to turn the heart of the father to the son and restore the tribes of Jacob. By Jesus' day, scribes taught that Elijah must come first (Matthew 17:10), and people wondered whether John the Baptist, or Jesus himself, might be Elijah (Matthew 16:14; John 1:21).
cultural:
The image of the sun rising with healing in its wings drew on a symbol well known in the ancient Near East, the winged sun disk, used in Egyptian and Persian art to represent divine or royal power and protection. Stamp impressions on storage jar handles from Judah in the time of King Hezekiah also bear a winged sun or winged scarab emblem. Malachi takes that familiar picture and applies it to righteousness itself, which will rise on the faithful like morning. The calves leaping from the stall are young animals released after being penned through the winter, a farmer's picture of pure, unrestrained joy.

Horeb in verse 4 is another name for Mount Sinai, where the law was given. The curse of verse 6 translates a word used for the ban, the setting apart of something for destruction, as with Jericho. In synagogue reading, it became Jewish custom to repeat verse 5 after verse 6 so that the prophets would not end on the word curse. Elijah remains present in Jewish practice: at the Passover meal a cup is set out for him, and a chair is set for him at circumcisions.
literary: The chapter has two parts. Verses 1 to 3 conclude the sixth disputation with a vivid contrast built on fire and sun: the same day burns the arrogant like stubble and rises like the sun on those who fear God. The phrases root or branch and ashes under the soles of your feet make the reversal complete, since those who seemed to prosper (3:15) are consumed and those who seemed to lose rise up. Verses 4 to 6 form a closing appendix, probably meant to end not only Malachi but the whole book of the Twelve and, many scholars think, the collection of the Prophets. The call to remember Moses points back to the Law, and the promise of Elijah, the great prophet, points forward, joining Law and Prophets as the two witnesses that prepare for the day of the LORD.

outline.t: The day burning like a furnace
The sun of righteousness for those who fear God
Elijah before the great day of the LORD

doctrines.note: The coming day brings a final separation. The arrogant and evildoers are consumed, and those who fear God are vindicated and healed, answering the complaint that serving God makes no difference.
The faithful are given something to wait for: the rising of righteousness with healing, and a prophet sent ahead of the day. Hope here is not optimism but confidence in a promise.
Elijah's mission is to turn the hearts of fathers and children to one another. Reconciliation within families is presented as a sign of God's renewal and as preparation for his coming.

words.note: Shemesh, sun. The same word names the sun in Genesis and elsewhere, and the sun was worshiped as a god across the ancient world. Malachi uses it as an image: God's righteousness will rise on the faithful like the dawn after a long night.

Marpe, healing or remedy. It can mean physical healing, but in the prophets it often means the restoration of a broken people (Jeremiah 8:15; 14:19). The righteousness God brings does not only judge; it mends.

Eliyyah, Elijah, a name meaning my God is the LORD. Elijah confronted Baal worship in the ninth century BC and was taken to heaven without dying. His name itself summarized his message, and Malachi promises his return before the great day.

Cherem, a thing devoted to destruction, the ban. It was used of cities such as Jericho given over entirely to God in judgment. The threat that God would strike the land with this ban shows how serious the hour is if hearts are not turned.

christ: The New Testament answers Malachi's final promise directly. The angel who announces John the Baptist's birth says John will go before the Lord “in the spirit and power of Elijah, to turn the hearts of the fathers to their children” (Luke 1:17). John dressed like Elijah (Matthew 3:4; compare 2 Kings 1:8), and Jesus said of him, “he is the Elijah who was to come” (Matthew 11:14), and again, “Elijah has already come, and they did not recognize him” (Matthew 17:12). If John is Elijah, then the one he prepared for is the Lord of the great day, and Jesus is that one. At the transfiguration Moses and Elijah, the two figures named in Malachi's last verses, appear with Jesus on the mountain (Matthew 17:3), as though the Law and the Prophets come to stand beside the one they were pointing to. Christians have also long heard the sun of righteousness rising with healing as a description of Christ, as in Charles Wesley's Christmas hymn Hark the Herald Angels Sing, though that is a thematic application rather than a New Testament quotation.

hard.q: Was John the Baptist literally Elijah, and is Elijah still to come?
hard.a:
Jesus says John is the Elijah who was to come (Matthew 11:14; 17:12), yet when John was asked whether he was Elijah he answered that he was not (John 1:21). Most interpreters reconcile these by Luke 1:17: John was not Elijah returned in person, and the Bible does not teach reincarnation, but he came in the spirit and power of Elijah and fulfilled the role Malachi described.

Christians differ on whether the promise has a further fulfillment. Some point to Jesus' words that Elijah does indeed come and will restore all things (Matthew 17:11) and to the two witnesses of Revelation 11, whose miracles echo Elijah's, as signs that an Elijah-like ministry will precede Christ's return. Others read Matthew 17:11-12 as saying the promise was fulfilled in John and see Revelation 11 as symbolic of the church's witness. Jewish tradition still awaits Elijah as the herald of the Messiah. On every Christian reading, John the Baptist is the one the Gospels present as Malachi's messenger.

questions: The same day is a furnace for some and a sunrise for others. What determines which it will be, according to this chapter?
Malachi ends by pointing back to Moses and forward to Elijah. Why might remembering and hoping belong together in a life of faith?
Elijah's work is to turn the hearts of fathers and children. What relationships in your family most need that kind of turning?
